headline: Two Senate debates, two nights, and one “Oh, shut up.”
summary: Alaska's Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola sparred Wednesday over the Iran war, prices and fisheries. In Maine on Thursday a protester shouted over Susan Collins, who called him one of Troy Jackson's supporters. "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." Maine is one of a handful of races that will decide the Senate.

cover_question.q: Why did he say shut up on TV?

cover_answer: He was annoyed, and no rule stopped him. Voters judge it.
table_question: Someone keeps heckling you. What's the best thing to say back?

5-7.script: Grown-ups who want to be senators argued on TV two nights running, in Alaska, then Maine. In Alaska somebody asked for decorum, a fancy word for manners. In Maine a man in the crowd kept shouting and one of them said "Oh, shut up," which you can't say at our table. Two kids wanting one swing while a third one yells. The voters there will pick.
5-7.why: The table rule they police, and a new word for manners.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and "shut up" is a rule they already enforce at home, so the script gives them the one rude line, a new word for manners and the swing, then hands the choice to the voters. Expect "does he get in trouble?" No time-out. The grown-ups vote instead.

8-12.script: Senate debates in Alaska and Maine both turned testy this week. In Maine a protester yelled, Susan Collins said he was obviously Troy Jackson's supporter, and Jackson said "Oh, shut up." A debate has a moderator but no referee. The voters score it in two weeks.
8-12.why: Two nights, two snaps, no penalty. The voters are the referee.
8-12.why_long: This age is checking whether adults keep the rules they set, and a candidate saying "shut up" on TV is what they notice. The script runs the chain twice, Alaska then Maine: a heated hour, a heckler, a snap, no penalty. No referee is the mechanism; the voters fill the job. Expect "who won?" Nobody scores a debate. The vote does.

13-17.script: Does a rude line cost votes or win them? Troy Jackson told Susan Collins "Oh, shut up" Thursday after she pinned a heckler on him. Second: asked when she stopped Trump and it changed the outcome, Collins named the Hegseth vote. The moderator said it didn't.
13-17.why: Rudeness as a tactic, and a record checked on air.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the line was rude, and it may have worked. The script asks that first, then hands them Collins's Hegseth answer and the moderator's live correction, a fact-check they can watch happen. Expect "would you have said it?" Answer honestly, then ask what they would have done with a heckler.

5-7.q: Why did he say shut up on TV?
5-7.a: A man in the crowd kept shouting and he got annoyed. It was rude, and everyone noticed.

8-12.a: A data-center protester, The Hill says. Jackson said he didn't know him.
Nobody scores it. The voters decide in just over two weeks.

13-17.q: Did "shut up" help him or hurt him?
13-17.a: Nobody knows yet. Axios says both sounded like kids on a playground.
Collins said she organized votes against Hegseth. One senator flipped. Hegseth got the job.
